questions.question: What is .NET, and how is it different from C#?
questions.answer: C# is a programming language. .NET provides the runtime, libraries and tools that run applications written in C# and other supported languages. ASP.NET Core is the web framework.
questions.example: C# source is compiled into an assembly; runtime services include garbage collection and execution. JIT commonly compiles intermediate code to machine code; AOT is another deployment option.
questions.mistake: Calling C#, .NET and ASP.NET the same thing.

questions.question: Modern .NET versus .NET Framework?
questions.answer: Modern .NET is cross-platform and is the usual choice for new ASP.NET Core services. .NET Framework is the older Windows-focused platform used by many existing applications.
questions.example: Ask whether the role uses ASP.NET Core or classic ASP.NET MVC/Web Forms. Migration can involve incompatible dependencies and hosting changes.
questions.mistake: Assuming a Framework application can always migrate by changing its target version.

questions.question: What are CLR, managed code and GC?
questions.answer: The CLR executes managed code and provides services such as memory management, exception handling and type safety. GC reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable.
questions.example: A static collection that keeps references alive can cause memory growth even with a garbage collector. External resources still require deliberate cleanup.
questions.mistake: Saying GC prevents every memory leak or immediately frees every unused object.

questions.question: Value types versus reference types?
questions.answer: Assigning a value type copies its value. Assigning a reference type copies a reference to the same object. Examples are int/struct and class respectively.
questions.example: Two variables referencing the same List see the same mutations. A struct can contain reference fields, so copying it need not deeply copy the object graph.
questions.mistake: Saying all value types are on the stack and all references are on the heap.

questions.question: What is boxing and unboxing?
questions.answer: Boxing wraps a value type value in an object representation. Unboxing extracts the value with the expected value type. It can create allocations and type-cast failures.
questions.example: object value = 42; int n = (int)value; works. Casting that boxed int directly to long fails; unbox to int first, then convert.
questions.mistake: Using non-generic collections unnecessarily when a typed collection is available.

questions.question: Why are strings immutable?
questions.answer: A string cannot be changed after creation. Operations that appear to modify it produce another string. Immutability makes sharing and reasoning about string values simpler.
questions.example: For repeated concatenation in a loop, StringBuilder can avoid many intermediate strings. For a few values, ordinary interpolation is clearer.
questions.mistake: Claiming StringBuilder is always faster for every string operation.

questions.question: Explain encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
questions.answer: Encapsulation protects state and valid transitions. Abstraction exposes useful behavior while hiding details. Inheritance derives from a base type. Polymorphism lets different implementations satisfy the same contract.
questions.example: A payment interface abstracts charging; a wallet class guards its balance; card and bank implementations behave differently through the same interface.
questions.mistake: Reciting definitions without showing how they affect an API or class.

questions.question: Interface versus abstract class?
questions.answer: An interface describes a contract and allows multiple interface implementations. An abstract class can share instance state, constructors and implementation; a class has one direct base class.
questions.example: Use INotificationSender for email/SMS alternatives. Use an abstract base when a genuine shared base behavior exists. Modern interfaces can also have default members.
questions.mistake: Saying interfaces can never contain implementations, or inheriting only to reuse a few lines.

questions.question: Overloading versus overriding?
questions.answer: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameter signatures. Overriding replaces a virtual or abstract base implementation using runtime polymorphism.
questions.example: Print(int) and Print(string) are overloads. Dog overriding Animal.Speak is an override. The new keyword hides a member rather than overriding it.
questions.mistake: Thinking changing only the return type creates an overload.

questions.question: Explain SOLID with practical examples.
questions.answer: SRP: one reason to change. OCP: extend behavior without repeatedly modifying stable code. LSP: substitutes preserve contracts. ISP: focused interfaces. DIP: high-level logic depends on abstractions.
questions.example: An order service uses IPaymentGateway; a new gateway implementation can be injected. Do not force read-only clients to implement write methods.
questions.mistake: Creating an interface for every class without a real boundary or testing need.

questions.question: Composition versus inheritance?
questions.answer: Composition builds behavior by collaborating with other objects. Inheritance models a substitutable is-a relationship. I prefer composition when capabilities vary independently.
questions.example: An order service has a pricing policy and notification sender. This avoids a growing tree of special-purpose order subclasses.
questions.mistake: Treating inheritance as the only way to reuse code.

questions.question: Dependency inversion versus dependency injection?
questions.answer: Dependency inversion is a design principle about depending on abstractions. Dependency injection is a technique for supplying dependencies from outside an object.
questions.example: A constructor accepts IClock instead of constructing a concrete clock. Production supplies a real clock; a test supplies a predictable one.
questions.mistake: Confusing the design principle with a particular DI container.

questions.question: Array, List, Dictionary and HashSet: when?
questions.answer: Array fits fixed-size indexed data. List supports dynamic indexed sequences. Dictionary maps unique keys to values. HashSet represents unique membership.
questions.example: Use Dictionary<int,int> for Two Sum value-to-index lookup; use HashSet<int> when only duplicate detection matters. Hash lookup is average O(1), not an absolute worst-case guarantee.
questions.mistake: Using a Dictionary when only membership is needed, or mutating keys in a way that changes their hash.

questions.question: IEnumerable versus IQueryable?
questions.answer: IEnumerable represents an enumerable sequence. IQueryable represents a query expression a provider can translate, for example into SQL. Which methods run where depends on the provider and query composition.
questions.example: Filter and project an EF query before ToListAsync. AsEnumerable switches subsequent LINQ operators to in-process enumeration; it does not by itself materialize every row.
questions.mistake: Assuming IQueryable always means SQL or that every C# expression translates.

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
questions.answer: Many LINQ operators describe work that runs when the sequence is enumerated. Materializers such as ToList create a result at that moment.
questions.example: Enumerating a database query twice may execute two database calls. Changing the source before enumeration can change the result.
questions.mistake: Assuming creating a query variable already fetched its rows.

questions.question: FirstOrDefault, SingleOrDefault and Any?
questions.answer: FirstOrDefault takes the first match or default. SingleOrDefault requires at most one match and throws if more exist. Any asks only whether a match exists.
questions.example: Use Any for existence checks. Use SingleOrDefault only when uniqueness is a real contract, ideally enforced by a database constraint.
questions.mistake: Using Count() > 0 for existence without considering the query cost.

questions.question: What are delegates, lambdas and events?
questions.answer: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a compatible method. A lambda is an inline function expression. An event exposes controlled subscription to notifications.
questions.example: A filtering predicate can be a lambda. An event publisher raises a notification to subscribers; long-lived publishers may retain subscribers if they never unsubscribe.
questions.mistake: Treating every callback as a separate thread.

questions.question: var, dynamic, nullable types and records?
questions.answer: var infers a compile-time type. dynamic defers member binding to runtime. Nullable value types represent a value or null. Nullable reference annotations support compiler analysis. Records provide value-oriented equality semantics.
questions.example: var count = 3 is still an int. A record is useful for a DTO, but a record class remains a reference type and can contain mutable members.
questions.mistake: Saying var is dynamically typed or that records are automatically deeply immutable.

questions.question: What do async and await do?
questions.answer: An async method can suspend at an incomplete await and resume when the awaited operation completes. A Task represents completion, not necessarily a dedicated thread.
questions.example: Awaiting an HTTP call lets the server avoid occupying a thread just waiting for I/O. Marking a CPU loop async does not make its calculations faster.
questions.mistake: Saying async always starts a new thread.

questions.question: Why avoid .Result, .Wait() and async void?
questions.answer: Blocking on asynchronous work can waste threads and may deadlock in synchronization-context environments. Task-returning methods allow callers to await completion and observe exceptions; async void is mainly for event handlers.
questions.example: An ASP.NET Core request should await its data call rather than block on Result. Thread-pool starvation can still occur even without the classic UI deadlock.
questions.mistake: Fire-and-forget work that silently fails after a request finishes.

questions.question: Task.WhenAll and CancellationToken?
questions.answer: WhenAll combines completion of independent tasks. CancellationToken communicates a cooperative cancellation request that operations must observe or pass onward.
questions.example: Parallelize independent remote calls within limits. Pass cancellation to HTTP and EF methods. Never start parallel EF operations on one DbContext.
questions.mistake: Assuming cancellation forcibly terminates all code or that unbounded concurrency is safe.

questions.question: Task.Run versus naturally asynchronous I/O?
questions.answer: Task.Run schedules work on the thread pool, which can help keep a desktop UI responsive during CPU work. Naturally asynchronous I/O does not need Task.Run around it.
questions.example: For expensive server jobs, use a bounded background worker or queue with appropriate capacity rather than spawning unlimited request-side tasks.
questions.mistake: Wrapping every database or HTTP call in Task.Run.

questions.question: How should you handle exceptions?
questions.answer: Catch exceptions where you can recover or add useful context. Use centralized API error handling for unexpected failures. Log diagnostic details internally and return a safe, consistent client error.
questions.example: Use throw; to rethrow while preserving stack information. Handle expected validation failures explicitly instead of using exceptions as normal control flow.
questions.mistake: Returning stack traces, connection strings or secrets to clients.

questions.question: IDisposable, using and garbage collection?
questions.answer: IDisposable provides deterministic resource cleanup. using ensures Dispose is called when leaving scope, including on exceptions. GC handles managed memory and is not a substitute for timely resource release.
questions.example: Use using for streams you own; await using for IAsyncDisposable resources. Let the DI container dispose services it creates within their lifetime.
questions.mistake: Calling Dispose on injected shared dependencies you do not own.

questions.question: Walk through an ASP.NET Core request.
questions.answer: The server receives the request, then middleware processes it in order. Routing selects an endpoint; authentication and authorization run as configured; the endpoint handles input and returns a response.
questions.example: Response processing unwinds through middleware that awaited the next delegate. A middleware can short-circuit the pipeline. See the flow page.
questions.mistake: Assuming every request always reaches a controller.

questions.question: Why does middleware order matter?
questions.answer: Earlier middleware wraps later middleware. Exception handling must be placed where it can catch downstream failures. Authentication should precede authorization.
questions.example: A typical protected API explicitly orders routing, CORS when needed, authentication and authorization before executing its mapped endpoints. Static/public endpoints need deliberate policy decisions.
questions.mistake: Copying one pipeline order without considering endpoint and hosting requirements.

questions.question: Transient, scoped and singleton lifetimes?
questions.answer: Transient creates a new instance per resolution. Scoped reuses an instance within a scope, commonly an HTTP request. Singleton reuses one instance for the container lifetime.
questions.example: Choose a scoped business service when it uses the request DbContext. A singleton must handle concurrent access safely.
questions.mistake: Thinking scoped means one instance for the entire application.

questions.question: Why cannot a singleton capture a scoped DbContext?
questions.answer: Its lifetime outlives the request scope, so it can retain the wrong context and share unsafe state across requests. Lifetime validation may reject this configuration.
questions.example: A background worker creates and disposes an explicit scope for each unit of work. It does not keep the scoped object after disposing that scope.
questions.mistake: Changing DbContext to singleton to silence a lifetime error.

questions.question: Controllers versus Minimal APIs?
questions.answer: Both define HTTP endpoints. Controllers offer an attribute-based organization and MVC features. Minimal APIs provide concise endpoint mapping and can also use services, filters and route groups.
questions.example: Choose based on application size, conventions and team needs. Business logic belongs in testable services rather than large endpoint bodies.
questions.mistake: Calling one approach inherently secure or production-ready and the other not.

questions.question: Model binding, validation and DTOs?
questions.answer: Binding converts request values into parameters or models. Validation checks whether input meets rules. DTOs define the external contract separately from persistence entities.
questions.example: An update DTO exposes allowed fields rather than accepting an entire User entity with an IsAdmin property. Controller APIs using ApiController can produce automatic validation responses.
questions.mistake: Assuming all endpoint styles and framework versions have identical automatic validation behavior.

questions.question: Authentication versus authorization?
questions.answer: Authentication determines who the caller is. Authorization determines what that caller may do. An authenticated user is not automatically allowed to access every resource.
questions.example: A valid token identifies a user; an ownership check still ensures the requested order belongs to that user. Policies can express permission requirements.
questions.mistake: Checking only whether the user is logged in.

questions.question: How does JWT validation work?
questions.answer: A bearer token is sent with the request. The API validates signature, issuer, audience and lifetime according to configured trust. Claims are used for authorization.
questions.example: Signed JWT payloads are usually readable, not encrypted. Use HTTPS and avoid storing secrets in claims. Revocation/refresh design needs separate consideration.
questions.mistake: Merely decoding a JWT and trusting its payload.

questions.question: Which HTTP status codes should an API use?
questions.answer: 200 for successful content, 201 for creation, 204 for successful no-content, 400 for invalid requests, 401 for missing/invalid authentication, 403 for denied access, 404 for not found, 409 for conflicts and 500 for unexpected failures.
questions.example: A created resource can return a Location header. A validation error should identify safe, actionable field errors.
questions.mistake: Returning 200 for every failure or exposing internal exception messages.

questions.question: CORS versus CSRF?
questions.answer: CORS controls browser cross-origin access to responses; it is not authentication. CSRF exploits automatically attached credentials, such as cookies, to trigger unwanted actions.
questions.example: Cookie-authenticated applications need an appropriate anti-CSRF strategy. Allowed origins should be deliberate; bearer token designs have different exposure, including XSS risks.
questions.mistake: Treating CORS as a firewall that prevents all non-browser callers.

questions.question: How do you prevent SQL injection and overposting?
questions.answer: Use parameterized database queries and validate allowed input. Use explicit DTOs and server-side authorization for changes. Never trust client-supplied role or ownership fields.
questions.example: Interpolated SQL APIs may parameterize values, but raw string concatenation is dangerous. Dynamic identifiers require allowlisting because parameters represent values, not SQL structure.
questions.mistake: Assuming an ORM makes every raw SQL string safe.

questions.question: PUT, PATCH, POST and idempotency?
questions.answer: PUT generally replaces a resource representation; PATCH applies partial changes; POST commonly creates or invokes an action. Idempotency means repeating a request has the same intended effect as doing it once.
questions.example: A payment API can persist an idempotency key with a request fingerprint and outcome under a uniqueness constraint. PATCH idempotency depends on its operation.
questions.mistake: Retrying a charge blindly or confusing idempotency with identical response codes.

questions.question: What does DbContext do?
questions.answer: DbContext coordinates queries, tracked entity changes and persistence in EF Core. It represents a short-lived unit of work and is not safe for concurrent use.
questions.example: Load an order, change a property, then SaveChangesAsync. Keep request contexts scoped; use a separate scope/context for a separate background operation.
questions.mistake: Sharing one context across threads.

questions.question: Tracking versus AsNoTracking?
questions.answer: Tracking queries retain entity change information for later updates. AsNoTracking avoids that tracking overhead for read-only entity results.
questions.example: For a read-only listing, project only needed columns into DTOs. Tracking is useful for a read-modify-save operation, so disable it deliberately rather than everywhere.
questions.mistake: Believing AsNoTracking makes an inefficient query automatically fast.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.answer: One query fetches a list, then an additional query runs for each item to load related data. Latency grows with the list size.
questions.example: Inspect SQL and use appropriate projection or eager loading. Large multi-collection joins can also over-fetch, so assess split queries and pagination when appropriate.
questions.mistake: Adding Include for every navigation without measuring result size.

questions.question: How do you handle concurrent updates?
questions.answer: Optimistic concurrency compares an original concurrency token during an update. If another writer changed the row, the update can fail with DbUpdateConcurrencyException.
questions.example: Use a SQL Server rowversion or another configured token. Reload/merge, reject with a conflict, or retry only when business semantics allow it.
questions.mistake: Silently overwriting another user or assuming every database has SQL Server rowversion.

questions.question: What are migrations?
questions.answer: Migrations describe incremental schema changes derived from model changes. Review the generated operations and apply them through a controlled deployment process.
questions.example: Adding a required column to a populated table may need a staged backfill. Plan backup, compatibility and rollback/forward-fix before production changes.
questions.mistake: Automatically applying destructive migrations from every application instance.

questions.question: How do you improve a slow database endpoint?
questions.answer: Measure timings and inspect generated SQL and the database execution plan. Reduce rows and columns, use appropriate indexes, avoid N+1 calls and page large results.
questions.example: Filter before materialization; use a stable unique ordering for pagination. Caching may help repeated reads but introduces invalidation decisions.
questions.mistake: Guessing that more application servers will fix a poorly indexed query.

questions.question: INNER JOIN versus LEFT JOIN?
questions.answer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows. LEFT JOIN also retains unmatched left-side rows with null values on the right. One-to-many matches can produce multiple result rows.
questions.example: List customers with no orders using a left join and an IS NULL check on the non-nullable order key. Moving right-side filters into WHERE can remove unmatched rows.
questions.mistake: Assuming a join always returns one result per left row.

questions.question: WHERE, HAVING and GROUP BY?
questions.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping. GROUP BY forms groups. HAVING filters groups based on aggregate results or grouping expressions.
questions.example: Find customers with at least three paid orders: filter status in WHERE, group by customer, then HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3.
questions.mistake: Using HAVING as a replacement for every ordinary row filter.

questions.question: What is an index, and what does it cost?
questions.answer: An index is an additional access structure that can speed suitable lookups, joins and ordering. It uses storage and adds maintenance cost to writes.
questions.example: A composite index can help a query filtering by customer and ordering by creation time; column order and database behavior matter. Check the execution plan.
questions.mistake: Indexing every column or promising every indexed query is fast.

questions.question: Explain ACID.
questions.answer: Atomicity: commit all work or none. Consistency: preserve defined invariants. Isolation: control interference between transactions. Durability: committed data survives according to the database guarantees.
questions.example: A bank transfer updates both balances in one transaction and enforces sufficient funds. Isolation levels affect which concurrent anomalies are possible.
questions.mistake: Confusing transaction consistency with distributed CAP consistency.

questions.question: Normalization versus denormalization?
questions.answer: Normalization organizes facts to reduce duplication and update anomalies. Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data for a measured read requirement.
questions.example: Separate customers from orders; add a reporting summary only if its performance benefit justifies keeping that summary consistent.
questions.mistake: Assuming joins are inherently bad or duplicate data is always wrong.

questions.question: Deadlock versus optimistic concurrency conflict?
questions.answer: A deadlock is a cycle of waiting for resources; the database usually chooses a victim. An optimistic conflict means a version check detected another update.
questions.example: Reduce deadlocks with short transactions and consistent access order. A bounded retry may be appropriate, but a concurrency conflict can require user resolution.
questions.mistake: Retrying every database exception forever.

questions.question: An endpoint is slow in production. What do you do?
questions.answer: Define the symptom and compare latency percentiles, traffic and errors. Trace a request across API, database and dependencies. Identify whether time is CPU, I/O, locking or queueing.
questions.example: Check recent deployments and query plans before changing code. Make one measured fix, then verify latency and correctness under representative load.
questions.mistake: Starting with random caching or rewriting the entire service.

questions.question: How should you use HttpClient?
questions.answer: Reuse connection management through a suitable long-lived client/handler or IHttpClientFactory. Configure timeouts and pass cancellation. Treat remote failures explicitly.
questions.example: A typed client can centralize an external API integration. Retry transient failures with limits; unsafe operations need idempotency before retries.
questions.mistake: Creating and disposing a new handler for every request or retrying payments blindly.

questions.question: When would you use Redis?
questions.answer: Redis can provide shared low-latency caching or other data structures across application instances. A cache-aside flow reads cache, falls back to the database, then populates cache.
questions.example: Set a TTL and define invalidation after writes. Plan for cache outage and hot-key/stampede behavior. Keep the authoritative data source explicit.
questions.mistake: Treating cached data as permanently correct or adding a cache before measuring.

questions.question: What is a background queue useful for?
questions.answer: It moves slow or bursty work out of the interactive request and allows bounded processing and retries. Return a job identifier when work is asynchronous.
questions.example: Generate a report in a worker, persist job status and let the client poll. Make consumers idempotent because messages may be delivered more than once.
questions.mistake: Claiming a queue alone guarantees exactly-once business effects.

questions.question: Explain a layered API architecture.
questions.answer: An endpoint handles HTTP concerns, an application service coordinates a use case, domain logic enforces rules, and infrastructure handles storage or external systems.
questions.example: Place business validation where it can be reused and tested. Small services can stay simple; extra layers should justify their maintenance cost.
questions.mistake: Adding repositories and interfaces mechanically when they hide useful EF capabilities without benefit.

questions.question: Unit tests versus integration tests?
questions.answer: Unit tests isolate small behavior with controlled dependencies. Integration tests verify collaborating parts such as routing, authentication, serialization and database behavior.
questions.example: Test a pricing rule in isolation; test an API update against a representative database provider. EF in-memory behavior is not a substitute for relational semantics.
questions.mistake: Mocking everything and never testing real persistence or authorization.

questions.question: How would you deploy a .NET API with Docker and CI/CD?
questions.answer: Build and test in CI, create a versioned image, scan/configure it and deploy with health checks and rollback capability. A multi-stage image separates build tools from runtime.
questions.example: Provide secrets at runtime and handle schema changes separately and safely. Confirm readiness before shifting traffic. Docker packages an app; it is not a virtual machine per container.
questions.mistake: Baking secrets into image layers or assuming a passing build proves production health.

questions.question: Logs, metrics and traces: why all three?
questions.answer: Logs describe events, metrics show aggregate trends, and traces connect work across a request path. Together they help identify impact and root cause.
questions.example: Use correlation identifiers and structured fields for an order request. Track latency, error rates and saturation; redact personal data and credentials.
questions.mistake: Logging entire request bodies or access tokens by default.

questions.question: HLD versus LLD for an order service?
questions.answer: HLD covers components, data flow, scaling and reliability. LLD covers interfaces, classes, schemas and detailed interactions within those components.
questions.example: Start with requirements; draw client, API, database and queue. Then detail PlaceOrder, stock checks, transaction boundaries and idempotency.
questions.mistake: Drawing microservices before asking about traffic, consistency and team constraints.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: I am a full-stack developer with around three years of experience. I work on [your real stack] and have contributed to [real feature]. My strengths are [evidence]. I am looking to deepen backend ownership in this role.
questions.example: Keep it to 60-90 seconds. Connect one feature, one technical decision and one outcome to the job. If .NET is new, say so and explain transferable backend experience.
questions.mistake: Inventing production .NET experience, company names or impact numbers.

questions.question: Describe a production issue or disagreement.
questions.answer: Use STAR: situation, task, action and result. Explain what you personally investigated or changed, how you collaborated and what you learned.
questions.example: For a disagreement: state the shared goal, evidence, trade-off and small experiment. Use a real example; mention the prevention step after an incident.
questions.mistake: Blaming teammates or claiming team work as entirely your own.

questions.question: What if you do not know an answer?
questions.answer: State what you know, clarify assumptions, and reason through the problem. Be honest about the gap and describe how you would verify the detail.
questions.example: Say: I have not used that feature in production. My understanding is ... I would verify it with a small example and the official documentation.
questions.mistake: Guessing confidently. Ask useful closing questions about their .NET version, database, testing and ownership expectations.

examples.title: 01 / Dictionary: Two Sum
examples.explanation: Assume non-null input; return indices for any valid pair, or an empty array if absent. [2,7,11,15], target 9 gives [0,1]. [3,3], target 6 gives [0,1]. Check before inserting so the same index is not reused. Average O(n) time and O(n) space. The long subtraction avoids int overflow.
examples.followUp: Why a Dictionary rather than HashSet? We need the earlier index, not only whether the complement exists.

examples.title: 02 / LINQ: paid orders by customer
examples.explanation: Assume orders is an in-memory collection with CustomerId, Status and decimal Amount. For paid amounts 10 and 20 for customer A, total is 30; unpaid orders are excluded. GroupBy creates groups; Select changes the shape. An EF query requires checking provider translation.
examples.followUp: What changes if orders is IQueryable? The expression may be translated to database operations before materialization.

examples.title: 03 / Async HTTP with cancellation
examples.explanation: The endpoint URL is illustrative. The caller supplies a configured client and owns its lifetime; this method owns the response. Non-success statuses throw. Cancellation propagates. In a real API, map dependency failures deliberately and configure timeouts.
examples.followUp: Why not Task.Run? The HTTP library already provides asynchronous I/O. Why not dispose client here? This method does not own it.

examples.title: 04 / EF Core: read-only page
examples.code:
var page = await db.Products
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(p => p.IsActive)
    .OrderBy(p => p.Id)
    .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
    .Select(p => new { p.Id, p.Name, p.Price })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
examples.explanation: Assume an EF DbContext with Products and validated bounded integers pageNumber >= 1 and 1 <= pageSize <= 100. Ordering is stable because Id is unique. Filtering and projection happen before materialization. For deep pages consider keyset pagination, such as Id > lastId.
examples.followUp: Do you need AsNoTracking for this scalar-only projection? No entities are materialized here, so there are no entity instances to track; it mainly communicates read-only intent.

examples.title: 05 / SQL: customers with three paid orders
examples.code:
SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS PaidOrders,
       SUM(Amount) AS TotalPaid
FROM Orders
WHERE Status = 'Paid'
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY TotalPaid DESC, CustomerId;
examples.explanation: Assume one row per order and non-null Amount. WHERE first keeps paid orders. GROUP BY builds one group per customer. HAVING retains groups with at least three orders. The second ordering key makes ties deterministic.
examples.followUp: If you need customers with zero orders, why is this query insufficient? Start from Customers and join Orders with suitable counting and filtering.

examples.title: 06 / Polymorphism and injection
examples.explanation: Assume non-negative amounts; real pricing also defines currency rounding and validation. Checkout depends on the contract rather than a concrete policy. TenPercent.Apply(100m) returns 90m. A different implementation changes the policy without changing Checkout.
examples.followUp: Which SOLID principles does this illustrate? Dependency inversion and open/closed design. Explain why you would avoid unnecessary abstraction for trivial, unchanging logic.
